title: Serialise changes to shared content
statement: When several people or agents change the same content, let them analyse in parallel but apply changes one at a time, and check the merge against every intended change.
example: Two audit lanes edited the same sentence array, and a later write silently overwrote a correct anti-gaming fix while local checks passed.
detail: In a case study of one Grade 3 reading lesson, two audit lanes edited the same sentence array, each change sound on its own, and a later write silently overwrote a correct anti-gaming fix; passing local checks did not detect the lost intent, and the fix was reapplied during the final diff review (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans-wiki/Peter-Pan-Quality-Case-Study-2026-08-24.md`, lines 254-262). Its durable rule is to parallelise analysis but serialise writes to shared learner content, and to require an intent-aware final diff for every merge, not just conflict-free bytes (same file, lines 264-265). The prevention it names is ownership of each path or field before editing, rereading the latest bytes before a patch, a post-merge diff against both intended changes and rerunning the checks the change invalidated (same file, lines 267-268).
against: The evidence is one lesson's case study, which says it is not a standard and is no evidence about lessons not inspected (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans-wiki/Peter-Pan-Quality-Case-Study-2026-08-24.md`, lines 4-5).

evidence.quote: A later write silently overwrote a correct anti-gaming fix.
Each lane’s proposed change was sound in isolation, but both assumed they owned the shared content surface.
Passing local checks did not detect lost intent.
Parallelize analysis; serialize writes to shared learner content. Every merge requires an intent-aware final diff, not just conflict-free bytes.
post-merge diff against both intended changes
